section_summary: This section concerns Japan’s 1934 Petroleum Industry Control Law and its effects on foreign oil companies. State Department conversations, company memoranda, cables, and embassy reports focus on storage requirements, gasoline quotas, licenses, and possible American, British, and Dutch responses. The documents also connect the dispute to a proposed oil monopoly in Manchuria and proposals to restrict crude-oil exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Walter C. Teagle on coordinated action over Japan’s oil law
subfiles.about: Teagle discusses British and Dutch approaches, oil sales to Japan and Manchukuo, and possible American representations.
subfiles.summary: The conversation considers coordination with Sir Henri Deterding and the British and Dutch governments. Teagle reports that American firms have temporarily postponed bids to supply Manchukuo, but says a wider agreement to withhold oil from Japan is impracticable.

subfiles.title: London message to Richard Airey concerning Dutch protest plans
subfiles.about: The Dutch government considers protesting Japan’s petroleum law and seeks the American position on simultaneous protest.
subfiles.summary: Reports Dutch concern over discriminatory quotas and possible coordinated protests.

subfiles.title: Copy of London message to Richard Airey
subfiles.about: A second copy reports Dutch plans regarding Japan’s petroleum law and discriminatory quotas.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate of the preceding confidential London message.

subfiles.title: Additional copy of London message to Richard Airey
subfiles.about: A third copy reports Dutch plans regarding Japan’s petroleum law and discriminatory quotas.
subfiles.summary: Another duplicate of the confidential London message.

subfiles.title: Telephone conversation with Walter C. Teagle
subfiles.about: Teagle and Hornbeck discuss whether Britain or the United States is expected to act next.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck explains that Washington has invited British suggestions but has received none. Teagle agrees to seek clarification from his London contacts.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Walter C. Teagle on petroleum strategy
subfiles.about: Hornbeck and Teagle discuss Japan’s oil law, foreign-company cooperation, and possible pressure through petroleum supplies.
subfiles.summary: At a September 18 meeting, Teagle reports continuing British deliberations. Hornbeck asks whether oil companies could warn Japan that onerous conditions might lead them to leave the market and restrict crude supplies. They discuss oil sources, comparable restrictions in France and Italy, and unanswered company questions to Japanese officials.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck note on Teagle’s memorandum
subfiles.about: Hornbeck links Teagle’s attached memorandum to draft telegrams for Tokyo and London.
subfiles.summary: Identifies the attached memorandum as a summary of the facts and problem.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Teagle and Swain on Japan’s oil law
subfiles.about: Teagle supplies a company memorandum while Hornbeck describes tentative American representations.
subfiles.summary: Teagle reports that the British Ambassador in Tokyo has been told to consult American and Dutch colleagues. Hornbeck reads a tentative passage on conditions that could prevent American firms from operating in Japan. Teagle submits the attached company memorandum.

subfiles.title: Memo re Petroleum Industry Control Law—Japanese Empire
subfiles.from: Standard Oil Company of New Jersey
subfiles.about: The company details its objections to Japan’s petroleum law and its effects on investment and trade.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes annual licenses, mandatory reserve stocks, government purchase and pricing powers, compulsory facilities, disclosure of business information, and control of operating plans. It estimates substantial added costs and argues that reduced gasoline quotas favor Japanese firms. It recounts unsatisfactory Japanese replies, decisions about a possible refinery, Dutch protest plans, and company losses.

subfiles.title: Extract of Rising Sun Petroleum letter to Japan’s commerce minister
subfiles.from: Managing Director, Rising Sun Petroleum Company
subfiles.about: Rising Sun requests assurances on refining, quotas, licenses, compensation, prices, subsidies, and capital withdrawal.
subfiles.summary: The company asks nine sets of questions about equal treatment and the financial risks of complying with the oil law.

subfiles.title: Conversation with B. Kleijn Molekamp
subfiles.about: Hamilton informs the Dutch commercial counselor of American representations concerning Japan’s oil law.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton outlines Washington’s warning that arbitrary quotas, required storage, and government purchase powers could make American operations commercially unsound. He also reports Dutch representations in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Walter C. Teagle on further action
subfiles.about: Teagle and Hornbeck review the absence of new diplomatic developments and possible oil-industry tactics.
subfiles.summary: They discuss difficulties in coordinating company action and consider sending senior oil-industry representatives to Japanese authorities. They conclude that immediate action would be premature.

subfiles.title: Japanese Oil Situation
subfiles.about: Sawyer reports Japanese oil purchases and summarizes the law’s reserve and government-purchase provisions.
subfiles.summary: Reports heavy purchases and the financial burden of required oil reserves.

subfiles.title: Coe letter forwarding Yokohama cables
subfiles.about: Coe forwards October 10 and 15 cables and comments on storage requirements and Japanese comparisons with French law.
subfiles.summary: Introduces the attached cables and promises further analysis.

subfiles.title: Yokohama cable on meeting with Vice-Minister Yoshino
subfiles.about: Yoshino addresses storage rules, gasoline quotas, written answers, and a possible refinery application.
subfiles.summary: Yoshino rejects changes to reserve rules but suggests quota adjustments and favorable consideration of a later refinery application.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Yokohama cable on meeting with Yoshino
subfiles.about: A second copy records Yoshino’s statements on storage, quotas, and a possible refinery.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate of the October 10 Yokohama cable.

subfiles.title: Yokohama cable on private discussion with Yoshino
subfiles.about: Yoshino discusses possible guarantees of business volume and foreign participation in future gasoline sales.
subfiles.summary: The cable reports possible multiyear assurances, a share in increased gasoline consumption, and press reports about alternative crude-oil sources.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Yokohama cable on private discussion with Yoshino
subfiles.about: A second copy reports Yoshino’s possible assurances and Japanese interest in new crude-oil sources.
subfiles.summary: Clearer duplicate of the October 15 Yokohama cable.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Coe’s October 17 letter
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges receipt of Coe’s letter and two Yokohama cables.
subfiles.summary: Thanks Coe for keeping the Department informed.

subfiles.title: Coe letter forwarding October 19 Yokohama cable
subfiles.about: Coe explains the company’s incomplete 1935 business plan and asks to hear of useful embassy reports.
subfiles.summary: Introduces the cable and describes unresolved storage-plan requirements.

subfiles.title: Yokohama cable on incomplete business-plan forms
subfiles.about: Japanese authorities demand missing business-plan information while the company awaits a diplomatic response.
subfiles.summary: Reports pressure to complete forms before the Petroleum Committee meets.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Coe’s October 19 letter
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges Coe’s cable and offers to share useful information after embassy despatches arrive.
subfiles.summary: Acknowledges receipt and promises relevant information if available.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram warning of an approaching oil crisis
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The embassy warns that Japan’s storage demands and Manchurian monopoly plans may require prompt American action.
subfiles.summary: Japanese officials refuse to postpone import and storage plans. The embassy fears that the Petroleum Committee may take drastic action against foreign companies and urges decisions before it meets.

subfiles.title: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Neville reports diplomatic representations, company disputes over storage and quotas, and a proposal to control crude-oil exports.
subfiles.summary: Neville describes his representations to Foreign Minister Hirota, planned British representations, foreign companies’ refusal to commit to six months of storage, and Standard-Vacuum’s protest over its gasoline quota. He argues that restricting crude-oil exports might induce Japan to ease pressure on foreign companies in Japan and Manchuria. He acknowledges that domestic, legal, and international obstacles could prevent such action.

subfiles.title: Text of American representations to Japan
subfiles.about: The United States expresses concern about oil storage, pricing, quotas, and investment security.
subfiles.summary: Requests relief from burdens threatening established American oil enterprises.

subfiles.title: Neville’s conversation with Foreign Minister Hirota
subfiles.about: Neville delivers American oil-law representations, and Hirota acknowledges the companies’ difficulties.
subfiles.summary: Hirota recognizes the hardship of costly storage without secure licenses or sales quotas.

subfiles.title: Standard-Vacuum request to postpone parts of its 1935 plan
subfiles.from: J. C. Goold, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: The company asks to defer storage, import, and stock details in its 1935 operating plan.
subfiles.summary: Requests postponement while the disputed requirements are under discussion.

subfiles.title: Standard-Vacuum protest against its gasoline sales quota
subfiles.about: The company requests reconsideration of its 96,000-kilolitre gasoline quota for the second half of 1934.
subfiles.summary: Standard-Vacuum argues that officials used temporary cartel quotas despite an earlier assurance that those figures would be ignored. It presents alternative sales calculations, says the allotment cuts its established trade and excludes it from rising demand, and warns of harm to its Japanese agents. The letter asks for a fair adjustment.

subfiles.title: Coe letter forwarding October 23 Yokohama cable
subfiles.about: Coe forwards copies of a Yokohama telegram concerning the oil situation.
subfiles.summary: Cover letter introducing the attached cable.

subfiles.title: Yokohama cable on worsening oil disputes
subfiles.about: The company reports embassy concern over an approaching crisis and continued Manchurian monopoly plans.
subfiles.summary: Urges action before the Petroleum Committee meets.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Coe’s October 23 letter
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges receipt of the October 23 cable on Japan and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Thanks Coe for continued reports on the oil situation.

subfiles.title: Japan: Government Oil Policy
subfiles.about: The report assesses Japan’s oil law as a national-defense and economic measure affecting foreign firms.
subfiles.summary: Despite severe OCR damage, the report describes state control of prices, reserves, and business operations. It interprets the law as part of Japan’s defense policy and economic development, with serious consequences for foreign oil companies.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Walter C. Teagle on Japan and Manchuria
subfiles.about: Teagle and Hornbeck consider Japan’s demands, the Manchurian monopoly, and possible restrictions on American oil exports.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says foreign companies must soon decide how to respond to Japan’s demands. Teagle revisits his proposal for American controls on oil exports; Hornbeck doubts the administration would take that course and urges Teagle to consult senior State Department officials. The conversation continues beyond page 74.
